text: Seeking clarification of the draft Law on Food Safety
The draft Law on Food Safety (revised) has yet to secure consensus among stakeholders.

Speaking at a review session on the draft Law on October 20, Mr. Nguyen Phuong Tuan, Deputy Chairman of the NA Committee on Science, Technology and Environment, warned that the lack of consensus could undermine implementation after the Law is adopted.
Among businesses' main concerns are additional administrative procedures and higher compliance costs.
Experts estimate that the resulting financial burden could reach trillions of VND.

Ms. Tran Ngoc Anh, representing a member enterprise of the Vietnam of Food Safety Science and Technology Association (Vinafosa), under the Vietnam Union of Science and Technology Associations (VUSTA), said lengthy licensing procedures increase costs, disrupt supply chains, and constrain product innovation.
One major concern is the proposed five-year renewal requirement, which could create recurring costs even for unchanged products with strong compliance records.
Though structured as a notification procedure, the requirement would still oblige businesses to monitor deadlines, prepare information, and complete the process for each product.
For products that have not changed, regulators should clarify why periodic reviews are necessary and which aspects need reassessment.
If renewal also requires new laboratory testing, costs could rise substantially.

Assuming a testing fee of VND20 million ($769) per application, renewing all 53,910 registrations filed between 2018 and 2022, provided they remain on the market and require new testing, would cost VND1.078 trillion ($41.5 million) per five-year cycle.
The draft does not explicitly require new test reports, making this a potential cost scenario that needs clarification rather than an established mandatory expense.
Another concern is that stability study reports could add hundreds of millions of VND in costs per product.
Under the associated draft decree, registration dossiers may require reports on product stability, including long-term studies to establish shelf life.

For a product with a 24-month shelf life, a new study involving three batches, each tested at seven intervals, could cost VND420 million ($16,154) in laboratory fees alone, assuming VND20 million ($769) per test.
This is an illustrative scenario, not a testing requirement or fee stipulated by the draft regulations.
The estimate excludes product samples, transportation, controlled storage, personnel, and report preparation.
If manufacturers' existing valid data are not accepted, they could face additional costs for new studies and delays in completing registration.
Stakeholders recommend assessing the necessity of these reports separately for each food category, accepting valid existing data and avoiding duplicate studies.
They also propose replacing blanket submission requirements with an obligation for businesses to retain shelf-life evidence and provide it when requested by regulators.
Licensing timelines present another challenge.
Under Article 45 of the draft decree, authorities would have up to 90 days for the initial assessment.
Each round of supplementary documentation could take another 120 days, comprising 60 days for businesses to provide additional information and 60 days for authorities to review it.
The draft allows up to two rounds.
The entire process could therefore take as long as 330 days, or approximately eleven months, excluding dossier preparation and without guaranteeing approval.
Ms. Anh noted that delays directly reduce the commercial value of food products.
A product with a 12-month shelf life, for example, would have only four months remaining for sale after two months of transportation and six months of administrative processing.
Vinafosa also questioned whether routine product improvements could become an additional administrative burden.
Food manufacturers regularly update formulations, flavors, specifications, and packaging to meet consumer preferences.
If even minor changes require re-registration, businesses could find themselves seeking approval for a new version shortly after receiving approval for the previous one.
The Association therefore recommended shortening assessment periods, setting a maximum timeframe for the entire licensing process, and establishing clear accountability for regulatory agencies.
Requests for supplementary documentation should be consolidated to avoid repeated submission rounds.
It also proposed replacing periodic renewal procedures with data updates and post-market supervision for unchanged products with strong compliance records.

The Ho Chi Minh City Food and Foodstuff Association, meanwhile, raised concerns over unclear criteria for mandatory product declaration registration under Clause 2, Article 46. In particular, the category of foods that "maintain, enhance, or improve human bodily functions" could be interpreted broadly enough to cover ordinary food products.
Article 74 of the draft Law establishes transitional deadlines of 24 and 36 months for businesses to complete or renew product documentation.

Within 36 months of the Law taking effect, businesses must complete product dossiers in accordance with Article 47, update records in the specialized food safety database for post-market supervision, and retain documentation at their establishments for provision to competent authorities upon request.
Separately, within 24 months, businesses must submit renewal notifications under Point a, Clause 1, Article 46.
Ms. Pham Khanh Phong Lan, NA Deputy from Ho Chi Minh City, noted that Decree No. 15/2018/ND-CP allows businesses to self-declare many conventional food products.
The draft Law shifts toward product standard declarations while requiring businesses to repeat procedures within the proposed transition periods.
According to Ms. Lan, more than 300,000 products have been self-declared in Ho Chi Minh City since Decree No. 15 took effect.
Requiring all these products to undergo new procedures within 24 months would create a substantial workload for businesses and regulatory agencies.
She recommended reconsidering re-registration and requiring new procedures only when products undergo changes to their ingredients or other information that warrants a revised declaration.
Ms. Lan also warned that additional licensing requirements would not necessarily improve compliance but could increase costs and create opportunities for misconduct during administrative processing.
Citing mandatory micronutrient fortification as an example, she argued that such requirements may benefit specific population groups but should not automatically apply to all products.
She further cautioned that stricter pre-market approval requirements could make licensing more difficult without necessarily encouraging businesses to improve compliance.
Lawmakers should instead reduce pre-market controls to create a more favorable business environment.

The appraisal report contained opinions recommending the abolition of the five-year validity period for product declaration registration certificates under Clause 2, Article 47. If retained, the NA Committee on Science, Technology and Environment proposed incorporating an online renewal notification mechanism directly into Article 47, without requiring businesses to resubmit technical dossiers or pay fees.
The effective date should also be aligned with Clause 4, Article 74 to ensure regulatory oversight while reducing the burden on businesses.
According to the Committee, the criteria for mandatory product declaration registration under Point a, Clause 2, Article 46 remains subjective.

Terms such as "health claims" and "maintaining, enhancing or improving bodily functions" could result in many products currently subject to self-declaration being transferred to the registration system, potentially overwhelming regulators.

It therefore recommended limiting mandatory registration to genuinely high-risk categories, including health supplements containing new substances or making claims to support disease treatment, medical nutrition products, and specialized nutritional products for children under 36 months and pregnant women.
Other categories should be subject to product standard declarations instead.
The Committee also recommended using risk analysis results as the basis for periodically reviewing and updating Appendices I and II.
Finally, mandatory re-registration or re-declaration should apply only to changes affecting product safety, intended users, or stated functions.
Minor technical changes should instead be subject to notification and self-updating mechanisms under Clauses 4 and 5, Article 46.
